name: Curcumin

angle.text: Users take curcumin to lower inflammation, ease joint soreness and exercise recovery, and reduce facial puffiness and skin redness. Trials cover joint pain and inflammation markers; the skin and appearance uses are lightly studied or anecdotal.

summary: Anti-inflammatory polyphenol. Absorption is poor without piperine or special forms.
currentQuick:
Curcumin is the main yellow polyphenol of turmeric (Curcuma longa). It is widely sold as a supplement and used in cooking and traditional medicine.
In recovery and appearance contexts it is taken for joint soreness, general inflammation and skin health. Systematic reviews report modest benefits for arthritis symptoms and inflammatory markers, though trial quality is mixed and plain curcumin is poorly absorbed.
How it works: Curcumin modulates inflammatory signaling such as NF-κB and COX-2 and has antioxidant activity in laboratory studies. Oral bioavailability is very low because of poor solubility and rapid metabolism, which is why piperine, lipid formulations and other delivery technologies are used.
Risks and caveats: Generally well tolerated, with occasional gastrointestinal upset. Rare cases of liver injury have been reported with high-bioavailability products, and it may interact with anticoagulants. Supplement quality varies, and adulteration with lead-containing pigments has been documented. Legal as a dietary supplement.
deepLead:
Curcumin is the principal curcuminoid, a yellow polyphenol pigment, of turmeric (Curcuma longa), a member of the ginger family. It is sold as a dietary supplement and cosmetic ingredient, used as a food flavouring and colouring (E100 in the European Union), and has a long history in traditional medicine .
In recovery, fitness and appearance communities, curcumin is taken for joint soreness, general inflammation, exercise recovery and skin health. Systematic reviews of randomised trials report improvements in pain and inflammatory markers in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis and reductions in markers such as C-reactive protein, although the quality of included trials is mixed and the reviews call for more rigorous studies . Wikipedia presents a more sceptical position, stating that extensive studies have failed to show medical value for curcumin and that its instability and low bioavailability make it an unlikely drug candidate .
A recurring theme in both the scientific and forum literature is absorption. Plain curcumin is poorly absorbed, rapidly metabolised and eliminated, which has led to formulations using piperine, lipids, micelles and other delivery systems . Curcumin is generally regarded as safe as a food additive, though rare cases of liver injury, interactions with medicines and adulterated products have been reported .

name: N-Acetylcysteine

angle.text: NAC is taken in appearance circles as an antioxidant for skin and acne, and by steroid users for liver support and recovery. It is established as a medicine for other conditions; small studies touch acne, while most other uses are anecdotal.

summary: Glutathione precursor with established medical uses.
currentQuick:
N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a modified form of the amino acid cysteine. It is an established medicine used as the antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose and as a mucus-thinning agent, and is also sold as a supplement.
In recovery and appearance communities it is used as a glutathione precursor and antioxidant. Beyond its approved uses, evidence for skin, hair or recovery benefits is limited, though it has been studied for psychiatric and compulsive-behavior conditions.
How it works: NAC supplies cysteine, the rate-limiting building block for glutathione synthesis, and can also act as a direct reducing agent and modulate glutamate signaling.
Risks and caveats: Common side effects are nausea and other gastrointestinal upset; a sulfur odor is commonly noted. Intravenous use carries anaphylactoid reaction risk. Its US regulatory status as a supplement has been disputed because it is also an approved drug, though it remains widely available.
deepLead:
N-acetylcysteine (NAC, acetylcysteine) is the N-acetyl derivative of the amino acid L-cysteine. It is an established medicine, used as the antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and as a mucolytic that loosens thick mucus in chronic lung disease, and it is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines. It is also widely sold as a dietary supplement .
In recovery, fitness and appearance communities NAC is used as a glutathione precursor and antioxidant, often as a liver-protection supplement during hormone or anabolic-steroid use, and sometimes for mood and compulsive behaviour. Its core medical uses are supported by clinical practice and trials. For other uses, including skin, hair and exercise recovery, evidence is limited: Wikipedia notes only preliminary research on androgenetic alopecia, and psychiatric uses are described as preliminary .
Common side effects are nausea and vomiting by mouth, and rash or a non-immune anaphylactoid reaction is possible with intravenous use . Its status as a supplement in the United States has been contested because it is also an approved drug .

name: Glycine

angle.text: Glycine is taken because it makes up much of collagen, with users hoping for better skin, hair and nails, and for its sleep effect. Sleep studies exist; benefits for appearance from supplementing glycine itself are untested and based on reasoning.

summary: Collagen's main building block. Cheap, safe, also helps sleep.
currentQuick:
Glycine is the smallest proteinogenic amino acid and makes up roughly a third of the amino acid residues in collagen. It is inexpensive, sold as a powder supplement, and consumed in the diet through gelatin and protein foods.
In looksmaxxing and recovery circles it is used to support collagen turnover and sleep quality. Small trials suggest improved subjective sleep, while direct evidence that supplementation visibly changes skin or connective tissue is limited.
How it works: Glycine acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem and, via NMDA receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, lowers core body temperature, which is the proposed route to better sleep. It is also a substrate for collagen, creatine and glutathione synthesis.
Risks and caveats: Very well tolerated at typical intakes; mild gastrointestinal upset or drowsiness can occur. It is a food-grade supplement with no particular legal restrictions. Interactions with some antipsychotics (e.g. clozapine) have been noted.
deepLead:
Glycine (Gly, G) is the simplest stable amino acid, with a single hydrogen atom as its side chain, and the only common amino acid that is not chiral. It is a building block of proteins and makes up about 35 percent of the amino acid content of collagen, where its small size allows the tight coiling of the triple helix . It is classed as non-essential because the body synthesises it, though Wikipedia notes it is considered semi-essential because the amount made may not meet all metabolic needs .
Beyond its structural role, glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem, a co-agonist at NMDA glutamate receptors, and a precursor for heme, purines, glutathione and creatine . It is inexpensive, available as a sweet-tasting powder supplement, and eaten in gelatin and protein-rich foods.
In recovery and appearance communities glycine is used to support collagen turnover, skin and joints, and sleep. Small human studies and a review by Japanese researchers report that glycine taken before bed improved subjective sleep quality in people with insomniac tendencies . Evidence that supplemental glycine visibly changes skin or connective tissue is indirect: trials of collagen hydrolysates, which are rich in glycine but contain many other amino acids and peptides, are not tests of glycine itself .

name: Taurine

angle.text: Taurine is used by lifters for endurance, cramp prevention and calming after hard training, and by steroid users for general protection. Exercise studies are mixed; its link to appearance is indirect and thinly studied.

summary: Cell-protective amino acid; thin evidence for appearance outcomes.
currentQuick:
Taurine is a sulfur-containing amino sulfonic acid found in high concentrations in muscle, heart, retina and brain. It is common in energy drinks and available as a standalone supplement.
In recovery and longevity discussions it is promoted for exercise performance, cell protection and general health. Reviews show small effects on some metabolic and performance outcomes, and evidence for appearance-related benefits is limited.
How it works: Taurine contributes to osmoregulation, bile-salt conjugation, calcium handling and antioxidant defense, and may modulate inhibitory GABA and glycine receptors. How oral supplementation translates to measurable benefits in healthy adults has not been well established.
Risks and caveats: Considered safe at typical intakes, with rare mild gastrointestinal effects. Most health concerns about energy drinks relate to caffeine rather than taurine. It is legal and sold as a supplement and food additive.
deepLead:
Taurine (2-aminoethanesulfonic acid) is a naturally occurring sulfur-containing compound found in high concentrations in muscle, heart, retina and brain. Chemically it is an amino sulfonic acid rather than a carboxylic amino acid, and because it is not incorporated into proteins it is classed as non-proteinogenic, though it is usually still called an amino acid . It is made in the human liver from cysteine and methionine, and is also obtained from meat and fish .
Taurine is a common ingredient in energy drinks, at roughly 1 to 3 grams per serving according to Wikipedia, and is sold as a standalone supplement . In fitness, recovery and longevity communities it is promoted for exercise performance, cramps, calming after training, sleep and cell protection; it is also taken by some people using anabolic steroids or other drugs as part of large supplement stacks .
Published reviews report small effects on some metabolic, cardiovascular and exercise outcomes, with limited and inconsistent evidence overall . Wikipedia states that high-quality clinical studies on possible effects of supplementation are absent and that preliminary human studies have been inadequate because of low numbers, inconsistent designs and varied doses . No study found in the sources reviewed tests taurine for facial appearance, skin or physique outcomes in healthy people.

name: Boswellia serrata

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles boswellia is taken to ease joint pain and speed recovery, so users can train harder and more often in pursuit of a more muscular physique. Trials have looked at osteoarthritis pain rather than training outcomes.

summary: Botanical studied for inflammation and joint symptoms.
currentQuick:
Boswellia serrata is a tree native to India whose resin (Indian frankincense) contains boswellic acids. Extracts are sold as joint and anti-inflammatory supplements, often alongside curcumin.
Its main evidence base is osteoarthritis symptoms, where meta-analyses report modest improvements in pain and function, though trials are small and often industry-linked. Relevance to appearance is indirect, via training recovery and joint comfort.
How it works: Boswellic acids, especially acetyl-keto-beta-boswellic acid, inhibit 5-lipoxygenase and reduce leukotriene production, and may suppress some inflammatory cytokines.
Risks and caveats: Adverse effects are generally mild, such as stomach upset or diarrhea. Product standardization varies, and safety in pregnancy has not been established. Legal as a dietary supplement; over-harvesting of wild trees is an ecological concern.
deepLead:
Boswellia serrata is a tree native to India and neighbouring parts of the Indian subcontinent whose gum resin, known as Indian frankincense, has long been used in Ayurvedic medicine . The resin contains pentacyclic triterpenoids called boswellic acids, including beta-boswellic acid and acetyl-11-keto-beta-boswellic acid (AKBA), which are the compounds most often used to standardise commercial extracts .
Extracts are sold as dietary supplements for joint comfort and general inflammation, frequently combined with curcumin, glucosamine, bromelain or fish oil. The best-studied use is knee osteoarthritis, where small randomised trials and meta-analyses report improvements in pain, stiffness and function over placebo . It has no established direct role in facial or body aesthetics; in appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a recovery and joint-comfort supplement for people who train.
Reviews describe the clinical literature as promising but limited by small sample sizes, short durations and frequent industry involvement in trials of branded extracts . Reported adverse effects are generally minor, such as gastrointestinal upset .

name: Bromelain

angle.text: Bromelain is taken to reduce facial puffiness, swelling and bruising, notably after surgery or injury. Studies have examined post-surgical swelling with mixed results; use for everyday facial puffiness is anecdotal.

summary: Pineapple enzyme studied for swelling and inflammation. Mixed.
currentQuick:
Bromelain is a mixture of protein-digesting enzymes extracted mainly from pineapple stem. It is sold as a supplement and used in food processing; a topical form is approved for debriding burn wounds.
In appearance contexts it is used to reduce post-procedure swelling and bruising (for example after cosmetic surgery) and general inflammation. Study results are mixed and often small.
How it works: Bromelain's proteolytic activity is thought to modulate inflammatory mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins and to affect fibrin breakdown. How much active enzyme survives digestion and reaches tissue after oral dosing is uncertain.
Risks and caveats: Side effects include stomach upset and allergic reactions, especially in people allergic to pineapple. It may increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants and interact with some antibiotics. Supplement potency is inconsistent. Legal as a supplement.
deepLead:
Bromelain is an extract from pineapple, mainly the stem, containing a mixture of protein-digesting enzymes and smaller amounts of other compounds . The best-known enzymes are stem bromelain and fruit bromelain, both sulfhydryl (cysteine) proteases . It is used industrially as a meat tenderiser and in baking and cosmetics manufacturing, and is sold as an oral supplement, often aimed at swelling, bruising and general inflammation .
According to Wikipedia, the only approved clinical use is a topical enzyme preparation, NexoBrid, authorised in Europe in 2012 for removing dead tissue from severe burns; for other uses, bromelain supplements are marketed without confirmed efficacy, dosage or interaction data . Systematic reviews of clinical studies cover surgery-related oedema and pain, osteoarthritis, and other inflammation-related conditions, with heterogeneous and often small trials .
In looksmaxxing and physique communities bromelain is discussed chiefly as a way to reduce swelling and bruising after cosmetic procedures, as a recovery aid for training, and as a digestive enzyme .

name: NMN

angle.text: NMN is taken, and sometimes applied topically, by people hoping to slow visible aging through higher NAD+. NAD+ biochemistry is well established; visible skin rejuvenation in humans is unproven.

summary: NAD+ precursor. The biochemistry is real; visible rejuvenation is unproven.
currentQuick:
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a nucleotide that the body converts into NAD+, a coenzyme central to energy metabolism. It is sold as an oral supplement, and its regulatory status as a supplement has been contested in the United States.
It is promoted for anti-aging, energy and skin appearance. Human trials show it raises blood NAD+ levels, but clear evidence of visible rejuvenation or lifespan benefit is lacking.
How it works: NMN is converted to NAD+ via the NAD salvage pathway; NAD+ is a cofactor for sirtuins and PARPs and for redox reactions. NAD+ levels decline with age in some tissues, which is the stated rationale for supplementation.
Risks and caveats: Short-term human trials report good tolerability, with mild gastrointestinal or flushing effects possible. Long-term safety has not been established, and theoretical concerns about NAD+ boosting in existing cancers remain unresolved. Product quality varies.
deepLead:
Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a biosynthetic intermediate in the production of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), a coenzyme involved in redox reactions and a substrate for signalling enzymes such as sirtuins and PARPs . In the body it is made from nicotinamide by the enzyme NAMPT, or from nicotinamide riboside by nicotinamide riboside kinases, and is converted to NAD+ by NMNAT enzymes . It is sold as an oral supplement and, in some products, as a topical skincare ingredient .
NMN is marketed for healthy ageing, energy and skin appearance, based on the observation that NAD+ levels fall with age in several tissues and that restoring them improves function in rodents . Human trials have generally reported that oral NMN raises blood NAD levels and is tolerated over weeks to months, with more mixed or modest results for functional outcomes; reviews state that evidence for anti-ageing effects in people is limited .
Its regulatory status in the United States has been contested: Wikipedia reports that the FDA determined in 2022 that NMN could not be sold as a supplement because it was under investigation as a drug, and later rescinded that determination for the beta-NMN form . In looksmaxxing and physique communities NMN appears as an add-on in longevity and recovery supplement lists .

name: Nicotinamide riboside

angle.text: Nicotinamide riboside is taken as an NAD+ booster by users aiming at slower aging and more energy, which they connect to a younger look. Human studies show it raises NAD+; effects on visible aging are untested.

summary: NAD+ precursor with human biochemical evidence; longevity unproven.
currentQuick:
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a form of vitamin B3 and a precursor to NAD+. It is sold as an oral supplement and has been tested in a number of human trials.
It is marketed for healthy aging and energy. Trials consistently show increased blood NAD+ levels, while reported benefits for muscle, metabolism or appearance have been modest or inconsistent.
How it works: NR is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases to NMN and then converted to NAD+, supporting sirtuin and DNA-repair enzyme activity.
Risks and caveats: Well tolerated in studies, with mild nausea, flushing or digestive effects at higher intakes. Long-term safety data are limited. It has GRAS status in the US and novel food approval in the EU; product quality varies.
deepLead:
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a pyridine-nucleoside and a form of vitamin B3 that serves as a precursor to the coenzyme NAD+ . Inside cells it is phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which is then converted to NAD+ by NMNAT enzymes, bypassing other known NAD+ synthesis routes . It is sold as an oral supplement under brands such as Tru Niagen and is closely related to, and often compared with, NMN .
NR is marketed for healthy ageing, energy and cellular health, on the premise that NAD+ declines with age and that supplementing precursors restores it . Randomised trials consistently show that oral NR raises blood NAD+ metabolites, but a 2023 review concluded that evidence that raising NAD+ improves physiological function in people is unclear . Trials in conditions such as mild cognitive impairment, Parkinson's disease, COPD, kidney disease and peripheral artery disease have mostly established safety and tolerability, with variable functional effects .
In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities NR appears in supplement lists, with some users reporting increased energy and others using it as part of longevity stacks alongside resveratrol and quercetin .

name: Resveratrol

chain: Slows cellular aging, lowers estrogen claimed
angle.text: Resveratrol is taken for anti-aging and for a claimed aromatase-inhibiting effect that would lower estrogen, and appears in some skincare. Lifespan findings come largely from lab organisms; human evidence for appearance is insufficient.

summary: Polyphenol studied for sirtuin signaling. Human longevity evidence insufficient.
currentQuick:
Resveratrol is a polyphenol found in grape skins, berries and peanuts, popularized by the "French paradox" and by early sirtuin-activation research. It is sold as a supplement and used in some skincare products.
It is promoted for longevity and skin health. Human trials show small effects on some metabolic markers, but evidence for longevity or visible anti-aging is insufficient, and its poor bioavailability limits interpretation.
How it works: Proposed mechanisms include activation of SIRT1 and AMPK and antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity. Some of the sirtuin findings have been disputed, and oral resveratrol is rapidly metabolized, leaving little free compound in circulation.
Risks and caveats: Usually well tolerated; high doses can cause gastrointestinal upset. It may interact with anticoagulants and drugs metabolized by CYP enzymes. Legal as a supplement; product quality varies.
deepLead:
Resveratrol (3,5,4'-trihydroxy-trans-stilbene) is a polyphenol of the stilbenoid class produced by plants such as grapes, blueberries, raspberries, mulberries and peanuts in response to injury or pathogens . Most US supplements are derived from the root of Japanese knotweed . It is sold as an oral supplement and is an ingredient in some skincare products, and it became widely known through laboratory reports that it activates sirtuins and extends lifespan in some organisms .
It is promoted for longevity, skin ageing, metabolic health and cardiovascular protection. Wikipedia states there is no high-quality evidence that it improves human lifespan or has a substantial effect on any human disease . Reviews of its pharmacokinetics describe about 75% oral absorption but extensive intestinal and hepatic metabolism, leaving oral bioavailability of the free compound below 1% .
In bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy forums, resveratrol is also discussed as a natural aromatase inhibitor and anti-inflammatory supplement, claims that are mainly anecdotal .

name: Spermidine

angle.text: Spermidine is promoted as an autophagy-inducing longevity supplement, with some users claiming it helps hair growth and aging skin. Human data are preliminary and focus on cognition and health markers; appearance uses are largely untested.

summary: Autophagy-linked polyamine. Preliminary human data.
currentQuick:
Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine present in all cells and in foods such as wheat germ, soybeans, mushrooms and aged cheese. It is sold as a supplement, often as wheat germ extract.
It is promoted as an autophagy-inducing longevity compound. Observational data link higher dietary intake to lower mortality, but randomized human evidence is preliminary and no cosmetic benefit has been established.
How it works: Spermidine induces autophagy in model organisms, partly through inhibition of the acetyltransferase EP300, and is required for hypusination of eIF5A, which supports mitochondrial function and immune cell activity.
Risks and caveats: Generally well tolerated at studied intakes; mild gastrointestinal effects are possible. Polyamines are also needed by rapidly growing cells, so theoretical concerns exist in cancer settings. Legal as a supplement or novel food in many regions.
deepLead:
Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine (C7H19N3) found in all living cells, first isolated from semen, and present in foods such as wheat germ, soybeans, mushrooms and aged cheese . It is a precursor to spermine and takes part in cell growth, membrane function and RNA and DNA stabilisation . It is sold as an oral supplement, often as wheat germ extract, and is promoted as an autophagy-inducing longevity compound .
Its profile rests largely on laboratory and animal work. A 2009 Nature Cell Biology paper reported that spermidine extended lifespan in yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells through autophagy, and a 2016 Nature Medicine paper reported cardioprotection and lifespan extension in mice . Observational data link higher dietary polyamine intake with lower cardiovascular and cancer-related mortality, but randomised human trials remain few and small, and no study has shown a cosmetic benefit in people .
Wikipedia also notes a laboratory finding that spermidine promoted hair shaft elongation in cultured hair follicles; this has not been established in clinical hair-growth trials . In bodybuilding forums spermidine is discussed as a longevity hack, typically via wheat germ .

name: Urolithin A

angle.text: Urolithin A is taken by people who want better muscle function and cellular health with age, which they link to physique and a younger body. Early human trials examined muscle endurance in older adults; appearance outcomes are untested.

summary: Mitophagy booster with early human trials (muscle endurance).
currentQuick:
Urolithin A is a metabolite produced by gut bacteria from ellagitannins in pomegranate, walnuts and berries. Only some people produce it efficiently, which is the rationale given for direct supplementation.
It is marketed for muscle and mitochondrial health in aging. Early randomized trials report improvements in some muscle endurance measures in older adults, while effects on strength and appearance are small or not shown.
How it works: Urolithin A is proposed to induce mitophagy, the clearance of damaged mitochondria, via PINK1/Parkin-related pathways, and to influence AMPK and other stress-response signaling.
Risks and caveats: Short-term trials report good tolerability. Long-term safety data are limited. It has GRAS status in the US, and regulatory status elsewhere varies. Most trials were sponsored by the commercial supplier.
deepLead:
Urolithin A is a benzocoumarin compound formed when gut bacteria transform ellagic acid and ellagitannins, polyphenols found in pomegranates, walnuts, raspberries, strawberries and oak-aged wine . It is not known to occur in any food itself, and how much a person produces depends on their gut microbiota, with efficiency varying widely and some individuals showing no conversion . Supplements providing urolithin A directly are marketed for muscle and mitochondrial health in ageing, the best known being a branded form called Mitopure .
Urolithin A was identified in 2016 as a first-in-class natural compound that induces mitophagy, the clearance of damaged mitochondria, in worms and rodents . Randomised trials in older and middle-aged adults have reported improvements in some muscle endurance and strength measures, along with safety and altered biomarkers, though effects on whole-body outcomes have been modest or mixed, and most trials were sponsored by the commercial supplier .
No published trial has tested urolithin A for facial or skin appearance. In training communities it is discussed as a mitochondrial and longevity supplement .

name: Coenzyme Q10

angle.text: CoQ10 is taken orally and applied topically by users aiming at younger-looking skin and more energy, and by some on statins to offset lower levels. Cosmetic evidence is limited; heart and statin-related uses are better studied.

summary: Electron-transport cofactor. Established physiology; limited cosmetic evidence.
currentQuick:
Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is a fat-soluble molecule that carries electrons in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and acts as an antioxidant. The body makes it, and levels fall with age and with statin use.
It is sold as an oral supplement and is added to some anti-aging creams. Evidence for cosmetic effects is limited and mostly from small or topical studies, while its best-supported uses concern cardiovascular and mitochondrial contexts.
How it works: CoQ10 shuttles electrons in oxidative phosphorylation and regenerates other antioxidants such as vitamin E. Topically it has been studied for reducing oxidative damage in skin.
Risks and caveats: Generally well tolerated, with occasional digestive upset or insomnia. It may reduce the effect of warfarin. Legal as a supplement; absorption varies with formulation.
deepLead:
Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10, ubiquinone, ubidecarenone) is a lipid-soluble benzoquinone made by the human body and found in meat, fish, seed oils and some vegetables . It is a cofactor in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, where it supports ATP production, and it also acts as a membrane antioxidant . The body synthesises it through a pathway that shares an early step with cholesterol, via HMG-CoA reductase, which is why statin drugs have been proposed to lower CoQ10 levels .
It is sold over the counter as an oral supplement and is used as an ingredient in some cosmetics and energy drinks, but Wikipedia notes it is not approved by the US FDA for treating any medical condition and that its manufacture is not regulated, so brands and batches may differ . The best-studied uses are cardiovascular, with the Q-SYMBIO randomised trial in heart failure being a frequently cited example, alongside statin muscle symptoms, migraine, Parkinson's disease and fertility .
In appearance contexts it is promoted for skin ageing, usually topically, and in training communities it is mainly discussed with statins, heart health and mitochondrial support .

name: Alpha-lipoic acid

angle.text: ALA is used by lifters and dieters for insulin sensitivity and carb handling, and as an antioxidant for general skin health. Glucose and nerve studies exist; appearance effects are thinly studied.

summary: Redox cofactor and antioxidant. Thin appearance evidence.
currentQuick:
Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) is a sulfur-containing cofactor for mitochondrial enzymes and a redox-active antioxidant, available as a supplement and in some skincare products.
Its best-established human use is symptom relief in diabetic neuropathy. Claims for skin and anti-aging benefits rest on limited evidence.
How it works: ALA and its reduced form dihydrolipoic acid scavenge reactive oxygen species and regenerate other antioxidants, and may influence insulin signaling and NF-κB activity.
Risks and caveats: Generally well tolerated; nausea, rash and, rarely, hypoglycemia in people on glucose-lowering drugs can occur. Legal as a supplement.
deepLead:
Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA), also called lipoic acid or thioctic acid, is an organosulfur compound derived from octanoic acid. It is made in small amounts by the body and serves as an essential cofactor for several mitochondrial enzyme complexes involved in aerobic energy metabolism. It is also sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement in the United States and as a drug in some countries, where it is marketed as an antioxidant and for glucose metabolism.
In Germany it has been approved as a non-prescription drug for diabetic neuropathy since 1966. Its evidence base in that condition is mixed: a 2024 Cochrane review of placebo-controlled trials lasting at least six months examined its effect as a disease-modifying agent in diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and secondary sources describe its conclusion as little or no effect on symptoms. Its use in anti-aging and skin-care contexts is more speculative; published reviews of antioxidants for skin health discuss it among many compounds, and no large trials of oral ALA for cosmetic outcomes were identified.
In longevity and body-composition communities, ALA appears mainly as a supplement for insulin sensitivity and nutrient partitioning, discussed on forums such as T Nation. Its pharmacology, particularly the difference between racemic and R-enantiomer products and the question of whether it acts as a direct antioxidant, is itself a matter of scientific debate.

name: Fisetin

angle.text: Fisetin is taken in longevity circles as a senolytic, with some claims of fat loss and skin protection from UV. Evidence is mostly animal and cell studies; human appearance effects are untested.

summary: Flavonoid senolytic candidate. Preclinical.
currentQuick:
Fisetin is a flavonol found in strawberries, apples and onions, sold as a supplement and discussed as a candidate senolytic, a compound that selectively clears senescent cells.
It gained attention after mouse studies reported extended health and lifespan. Human data are limited to early or ongoing trials, and no appearance benefit has been demonstrated.
How it works: In cell and mouse studies fisetin reduced senescent-cell burden and inflammatory signaling, possibly via pathways involving PI3K/AKT and mTOR modulation, along with antioxidant effects.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data at the doses discussed online are sparse. Possible interactions with drugs are not well characterized. Legal as a supplement, but not an approved therapy for any condition.
deepLead:
Fisetin (3,3',4',7-tetrahydroxyflavone) is a plant flavonol in the polyphenol family. It occurs as a yellow pigment in fruits and vegetables such as strawberries, apples, persimmons, onions and cucumbers, and its chemical formula was first described by the Austrian chemist Josef Herzig in 1891. It is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement and is discussed in longevity communities as a candidate senolytic, a compound proposed to selectively clear senescent cells.
Interest rose after a 2018 EBioMedicine paper reported that fisetin acted as a senotherapeutic that extended health and lifespan in mice. Human data remain limited to small or early-phase trials, several of them registered but not yet reporting, and Wikipedia states that there was no clinical evidence of benefit to human health as of 2018. No published human trial has tested fisetin for skin, hair or facial appearance outcomes.
Fisetin is a supplement and not an approved therapy for any condition. Research reviews describe its oral bioavailability as low, and efforts to improve absorption through new formulations are under way.

name: Quercetin

angle.text: Quercetin is taken as an antioxidant and, with dasatinib in research, as a senolytic, and is mentioned for puffiness and skin inflammation. Senolytic work is early; appearance-specific effects are untested.

summary: Antioxidant flavonoid with investigational senolytic effects.
currentQuick:
Quercetin is a plant flavonol abundant in onions, capers and apples, sold as a supplement. It is also the 'Q' in the dasatinib plus quercetin senolytic combination studied in aging research.
Human evidence for benefits is limited and mixed, covering blood pressure, allergy and inflammation. Cosmetic benefits have not been established.
How it works: Quercetin has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity and stabilizes mast cells in laboratory studies. In senolytic research it is paired with dasatinib to clear senescent cells in preliminary human work. Oral bioavailability is low.
Risks and caveats: Usually well tolerated at supplemental doses; high doses may cause headache or stomach upset and could affect kidney function or drug metabolism. Legal as a supplement.
deepLead:
Quercetin is a plant flavonol in the polyphenol group of flavonoids. It occurs in many fruits, vegetables, leaves, seeds and grains, with capers, red onions and kale among the foods containing appreciable amounts, and it is used as an ingredient in dietary supplements, beverages and foods. The name has been used since 1857 and derives from the Latin for oak forest, after the genus Quercus. Average dietary intake is estimated at 25 to 50 mg per day.
In longevity research quercetin is best known as the "Q" in dasatinib plus quercetin (D+Q), the first widely studied senolytic combination, which aims to remove senescent cells. Small early-phase human trials of D+Q have been run in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, diabetic kidney disease, Alzheimer's disease and bone loss after menopause, but those studies use quercetin together with a cancer drug and cannot show what quercetin alone does. Supplements are also marketed for inflammation, allergy and general health, and Wikipedia states that there is no high-quality evidence that quercetin in supplements or food treats cancer or any other disease.
Oral absorption is poor. One reference account concludes that bioavailability is likely below 1 percent and cautions that effects seen in vitro are unlikely to carry over to the body because of rapid metabolism. No clinical study of quercetin for skin, hair or facial appearance was identified.

name: Rapamycin

angle.text: Rapamycin is used off-label by longevity enthusiasts to slow aging, and topically in skin rejuvenation experiments. Lifespan extension is shown in animals; human longevity and cosmetic effects are unproven, and it is an immunosuppressant with known side effects.

summary: mTOR inhibitor at the center of aging research. Human longevity unproven.
currentQuick:
Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a macrolide originally found in a soil bacterium from Easter Island. It is a prescription immunosuppressant used in transplantation and certain rare diseases.
It is the best-replicated lifespan-extending drug in mice, which has driven off-label interest in humans. Human anti-aging benefit is unproven, and a systematic review of human data found limited evidence.
How it works: Rapamycin inhibits mTORC1 (and with chronic use, to some extent mTORC2), a nutrient-sensing growth pathway, which promotes autophagy and reduces protein synthesis and cell growth signaling.
Risks and caveats: Prescription-only. Known adverse effects include mouth ulcers, impaired wound healing, elevated lipids, glucose intolerance and increased infection risk, particularly at transplant doses. Off-label use for longevity is unapproved; physician supervision is advised in medical guidance.

It was first isolated in the early 1970s from a soil sample taken on Easter Island (Rapa Nui), which gave the compound its name. It was first studied as an antifungal, but its potent immunosuppressive and antiproliferative properties, which arise from inhibiting the kinase mTOR, redirected its development.
It is a prescription drug used to prevent organ transplant rejection (particularly in kidney transplantation), to treat the rare lung disease lymphangioleiomyomatosis, to coat coronary stents, and, in a protein-bound form, to treat a rare tumour called PEComa. It is also used in vascular malformations and, topically, for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis complex. Because inhibiting mTOR extends lifespan in several animal species, rapamycin has become the most discussed prescription drug in longevity communities, where some people use it off-label.

name: Metformin

chain: Less belly fat, possibly clearer skin
angle.text: Metformin is used off-label by some users for belly fat, carb sensitivity, acne and anti-aging, and to manage blood sugar during hormone use. It is established for diabetes; appearance uses are lightly studied, and some report it may blunt muscle growth.

summary: Diabetes drug with AMPK-related metabolic effects. Longevity unproven.
currentQuick:
Metformin is a first-line oral drug for type 2 diabetes, with decades of safety data. It is available by prescription.
It is discussed in longevity circles because of observational links to lower mortality and cancer rates in diabetics. Whether it slows aging in healthy people is unproven, and recent reviews express skepticism.
How it works: Metformin reduces hepatic glucose production and improves insulin sensitivity, partly through AMPK activation and mitochondrial complex I inhibition, with downstream effects on mTOR signaling.
Risks and caveats: Common side effects are gastrointestinal upset and vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use; rare lactic acidosis occurs mainly with kidney impairment. Some evidence suggests it may blunt exercise adaptations. Prescription-only; off-label use for aging is not approved.

Metformin, sold under the brand name Glucophage among others, is a biguanide medication taken by mouth and the main first-line drug for type 2 diabetes, particularly in people who are overweight. It is also used in polycystic ovary syndrome (which Wikipedia terms polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome) and sometimes off-label to limit metabolic effects of antipsychotic drugs. It was first described in the scientific literature in 1922 by Emil Werner and James Bell, studied in humans by the French physician Jean Sterne in the 1950s, and introduced as a medication in France in 1957. It is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines and in 2023 was the third most commonly prescribed medication in the United States.
Metformin is discussed in longevity and body-composition communities because observational studies in diabetics have linked it to lower cancer risk and mortality, and because its proposed mechanisms (AMPK activation, effects on mTOR signalling, reduced insulin) overlap with those studied in ageing research. Whether it slows ageing in people without diabetes is unproven, and reviews published in 2021 and 2025 take a cautious or critical view of the evidence.
It is a prescription drug in the US, UK and EU. name: Epitalon

angle.text: Epitalon is promoted as a telomere-lengthening peptide that slows aging, which users connect to a younger appearance. Research comes mainly from one Russian group; reliable human evidence for anti-aging or appearance is lacking.

summary: Telomere-hype peptide. No reliable human anti-aging evidence.
currentQuick:
Epitalon (epithalon) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) developed from an extract of bovine pineal gland by a Russian research group. It is sold as a research chemical.
It is popular in anti-aging communities because of claims that it lengthens telomeres. Most data come from the originating group, animal studies and cell lines, with no large independent human trials.
How it works: Cell studies report that epitalon can upregulate telomerase or alternative lengthening of telomeres, and it has been proposed to affect melatonin production and gene expression. Whether these mechanisms translate into human anti-aging effects has not been validated.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data are small and mostly from one research group. It is not approved as a drug by major regulators, product quality is unregulated, and telomerase activation raises theoretical cancer concerns.
deepLead:
Epitalon, also spelled epithalon or epithalone, is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the amino acid sequence alanine-glutamic acid-aspartic acid-glycine (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly, AEDG) and the molecular formula C14H22N4O9. It was designed from the amino acid composition of epithalamin, an extract of bovine pineal gland, and has been described as the putative active component of that preparation. Most of the research on epitalon and epithalamin comes from the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, led by Vladimir Khavinson, although laboratories elsewhere have recently begun to study it.
It is promoted in anti-ageing circles for claims that it activates telomerase and lengthens telomeres. Laboratory work reports that it increases telomere length in human cell lines through telomerase upregulation or an alternative lengthening mechanism, and Russian clinical reports claim effects on ageing markers. Independent, large, placebo-controlled human trials are lacking, and a 2026 narrative review evaluates mechanistic, preclinical and clinical evidence for the synthetic peptide separately from the older extract.
Epitalon is not approved as a drug by major regulators and is sold as a research chemical. On forums such as T Nation, it appears in peptide stacks discussed by members using unregulated products, an area in which product quality and dosing are not independently verified.

name: MOTS-c

angle.text: MOTS-c is used in peptide stacks as an exercise mimetic that users hope will burn fat and reverse age-related decline, sometimes alongside GLP-1 drugs. Evidence is preclinical, with little human data for appearance.

summary: Mitochondria-derived peptide studied for metabolic signaling. Preclinical.
currentQuick:
MOTS-c is a short peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA, first described in 2015. It is sold as a research chemical.
In mouse studies it improved insulin sensitivity and metabolic health, and it is promoted for fat loss, endurance and longevity. Human evidence is limited mainly to observational data and early-phase work on analogs.
How it works: MOTS-c is reported to act on the folate-methionine cycle and activate AMPK, shifting cellular metabolism, and may move to the nucleus under stress to regulate gene expression.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data are essentially absent for vendor products. It is not an approved drug and is prohibited by anti-doping agencies; purity and identity of gray-market peptides are unreliable.
deepLead:
MOTS-c (mitochondrial open reading frame of the 12S rRNA-c) is a 16-amino-acid peptide, with the sequence MRWQEMGYIFYPRKLR, encoded in humans by the mitochondrial MT-RNR1 gene. It belongs to the mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs), short peptides encoded by small open reading frames in mitochondrial DNA, of which eight have been identified. It is believed to take part in the regulation of glucose metabolism by skeletal muscle, rises with exercise, and is described as an exercise mimetic.
A team led by Changhan Lee in Pinchas Cohen's laboratory at the University of Southern California described it in 2015 in Cell Metabolism, reporting in mice that it promoted metabolic homeostasis and reduced obesity and insulin resistance. Later work linked it to physical fitness, reduced obesity and longer healthy lifespan in mice, and showed that it moves to the cell nucleus under metabolic stress to influence gene expression.
MOTS-c is not approved to treat any medical condition. The World Anti-Doping Agency named it explicitly as prohibited beginning in 2024, and Wikipedia reports its use as an injectable supplement within a "peptide stacking" trend despite the lack of robust human data. Published human data are limited to observational studies of circulating levels and exercise responses, with early-phase studies of a synthetic analogue and a registered phase 2 trial in prediabetes.

name: SS-31

angle.text: SS-31 is used by some peptide enthusiasts for mitochondrial support, cosmetic skin anti-aging and wound healing. It is approved only for Barth syndrome; cosmetic use is untested, and vendor products may differ from the approved drug.

summary: Mitochondria-targeted peptide in disease research. No proven cosmetic anti-aging.
currentQuick:
SS-31 (elamipretide) is a synthetic tetrapeptide that targets mitochondria. It has been developed as a drug for rare mitochondrial disease, and gray-market versions circulate as research chemicals.
In longevity discussions it is promoted for energy and anti-aging. Evidence is from disease trials and animal aging studies; no cosmetic anti-aging benefit in healthy people has been demonstrated.
How it works: SS-31 binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane, which is thought to stabilize respiratory complexes, improve electron transport efficiency and reduce reactive oxygen species production.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse events in trials are mostly injection-site reactions. Long-term safety has not been fully established, and vendor products are unregulated. Any regulatory approval concerns specific rare diseases, not general use.
deepLead:
SS-31, also called elamipretide (brand name Forzinity), is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted tetrapeptide developed by Stealth BioTherapeutics. It binds cardiolipin, a phospholipid found on the inner mitochondrial membrane, and is given by subcutaneous injection as the hydrochloride salt. In September 2025 the US Food and Drug Administration granted it accelerated approval, as a first-in-class medicine, for improving muscle strength in people with Barth syndrome who weigh at least 30 kg; Barth syndrome is a rare, life-threatening mitochondrial disease that mostly affects males.
Before that approval it was studied in primary mitochondrial myopathy, heart failure, age-related macular degeneration and other conditions, with mixed results. Its approval concerns one rare disease. It has not been approved for general anti-ageing, energy or appearance purposes, and no published trial has tested it in healthy people for those goals.
Outside clinical development, SS-31 circulates in peptide-using communities as a research chemical, where it is promoted for energy and longevity. Material sold this way is unregulated, and the clinical safety data come from supervised trials of the pharmaceutical product in patients with disease.
